title: Hearsay and inference
seoTitle: Turkish -mış past tense: hearsay and inference
intro: In [A2 unit 2](a2-u02-grammar) you met `-mIş` as the voice of news, discoveries and folk tales. This unit gives it in full: every person, the negative and the question (*gelmemiş*, *gelmiş mi?*), how to choose between `-DI` and `-mIş`, the reported forms of the other tenses (*geliyormuş*, *gelecekmiş*), and `-mIş` as an adjective (*pişmiş tavuk*, cooked chicken).

blocks.text: `-mIş` goes on the verb stem with four-way harmony, and takes the type I endings, those of **to be**: *gelmişim, gelmişsin, gelmiş*. It begins with a consonant, so the stem never changes (*gitmiş, yemiş, demiş*). Turkish grammars call it the learned past, *öğrenilen geçmiş zaman*: the speaker learned of the event, by hearing, by inference or by discovery, rather than seeing it happen.

blocks.text: The negative `-mA` comes before `-mIş`, and `-mIş` follows its vowel: *gelmemiş*, *yapmamış*, *görmemiş*. In a question, `mI` comes after `-mIş` and carries the ending, as in the present: *gelmiş misin?*, but *gelmişler mi?* The negative question is *gelmemiş mi?* (hasn't he come, then?).
Each person has its favourite use:

items: **I**: something you realize only now, or don't remember doing: *Anahtarımı evde unutmuşum* (I've left my key at home, I've just realized), *Uyumuşum* (I must have dozed off).
**You**: surprise at what you notice, or something you were told about the listener: *Çok değişmişsin!* (You've changed so much!), *İzmir'e taşınmışsınız* (I hear you've moved to Izmir).
**He, she, they**: hearsay and inference, the commonest use: *Ayşe partiye gelmemiş* (Ayşe didn't come to the party, I hear).
**Questions** ask for what the listener knows or can find out: *Bakalım, mektup gelmiş mi?* (Let's see whether the letter has come.)

items.en: You've changed so much!
Ayşe didn't come to the party, I hear.
I've left my key at home (I've just realized).
Let's see, has it snowed?
Your hair has grown!
The children haven't done their homework, it seems.

blocks.title: Unuttum or unutmuşum?
blocks.text: Both are correct. *Unuttum* simply states that you forgot; *unutmuşum* adds that you have only just noticed. The same goes for *Çok değiştin* and *Çok değişmişsin*: the second carries the surprise of seeing it.
`mI` comes after `-mIş`, never before it: *gelmiş mi?*, not *gel mi miş?* And the ending moves onto `mI`: *gelmiş misin?*, not *gelmişsin mi?*

Every Turkish sentence about the past makes a choice that English leaves open. `-DI` presents what you saw, did, or state as known fact. `-mIş` presents what reached you some other way: someone told you, you read it, you worked it out from the signs, or you just found out.

blocks.text: **In a story**, the choice tells the listener how you know each part. *Dün akşam Ali'yi gördüm. Çok yorgundu. Meğer sabaha kadar çalışmış.* (I saw Ali last night. He was very tired. It turns out he had worked until the morning.) The first two sentences are what you saw; the third is what you learned afterwards, and *meğer* (it turns out) often marks it.

**History and established facts** take `-DI`, though nobody alive saw them: *Fatih Sultan Mehmet İstanbul'u 1453'te aldı.* **Legends, tales and stories you can't vouch for** take `-mIş`: *Efsaneye göre Hezarfen Galata Kulesi'nden Üsküdar'a uçmuş* (According to legend, Hezarfen flew from the Galata Tower to Üsküdar). The [interlude](b1-u03-culture) of this unit tells that story.

**With I**, `-DI` is the default: *Dün sinemaya gittim.* `-mIş` means you didn't know or don't remember: *Annem anlattı: çocukken bu köye gelmişim* (My mother told me: I came to this village as a child).

items.en: I watched the match: Turkey won.
I read it in the paper: Turkey won.
The ground is wet; it must have rained.
It turns out he lied to me.
The door's open! A burglar has been in!

blocks.text: English and French mark hearsay with words when they bother at all: **apparently**, **I hear**, **it turns out**, *paraît-il*, *il paraît que*. Turkish marks it in the verb, and must choose every time.
Passing on rumours with `-DI` makes you vouch for them. If you only heard that the company is closing, *Şirket kapandı* says you know it for a fact; *Şirket kapanmış* says you heard it.

Any tense can be reported. Instead of the past `-(y)DI` of [B1 unit 1](gp-di-compounds), add the reported **to be** of [A2 unit 2](gp-idi-imis), `-(y)mIş`, and the type I endings: *geliyor* → *geliyormuş* (he's coming, they say), *gelecek* → *gelecekmiş* (he'll come, apparently). Turkish grammars call these *rivayet birleşik zamanı*, the reported compound.

blocks.text: The rules are those of every compound: the negative stays inside the verb (*gelmiyormuş*, *gelmeyecekmiş*), `mI` comes right after the tense and takes the buffer y (*Geliyor muymuş?* Is he coming, did they say?), and *they* puts *-lAr* before `-mIş` (*geliyorlarmış*), though *geliyormuşlar* is also common.
**`-mIşmIş`** is the colloquial double: the speaker passes on a report and doubts it, or finds it ironic. *Ali sınavı geçmişmiş* is **Ali has supposedly passed the exam**, said with a raised eyebrow.

**`-(I)rmIş`** is the habit of a folk tale: *Keloğlan her gün ormana gidermiş* (Every day Keloğlan would go to the forest). Outside tales, it reports a habit you only heard about: *Dedem her sabah beşte kalkarmış* (My grandfather used to get up at five every morning, they say).

items.en: It's going to snow tomorrow, they say.
Ayşe is working at a new job, I hear.
Ali called: he's going to be a bit late.
You're supposed to take this medicine after meals.
My grandfather used to get up at five every morning, they say.
Is he coming tomorrow, did he say?

blocks.title: Passing on a message
blocks.text: On the phone and in messages, the reported forms are how Turkish passes on what someone said: *Ali aradı, biraz geç kalacakmış* (Ali called; he's going to be a bit late). There's no need for **he said that**.
*Gelecekmiş* can mean **he'll come, they say** or **he was going to come, apparently**. Context decides, as it does for *hastaymış*.

Before a noun, a verb in `-mIş` works like an English past participle: it describes the result of a finished change. *Pişmiş tavuk* is **cooked chicken**, chicken that has cooked; *donmuş göl* a **frozen lake**. It takes no personal ending and doesn't report hearsay.

Some have become nouns. A *dolmuş*, from *dolmak* (to fill up), is a shared minibus taxi that leaves once it has filled up. *Geçmiş*, from *geçmek* (to pass), is **the past**, and you know it from the wish *Geçmiş olsun* of [A2 unit 7](gp-set-wishes).

Many `-mIş` adjectives are built on passive verbs, which [B1 unit 10](gp-passive) explains: *kırılmış bardak* (a broken glass), *haşlanmış yumurta* (a boiled egg). For now, learn to recognize them. And in [B1 unit 5](gp-participle-an) you'll meet `-(y)An`, which describes a noun by what it is doing: *pişen yemek* is food that is cooking, *pişmiş yemek* food that has cooked.

items.tr: Masada pişmiş tavuk ve pilav vardı.

items.en: There was cooked chicken and rice on the table.
I have toast for breakfast.
In winter we walked on the frozen lake.
We went to Taksim by dolmuş.
The past is in the past.

blocks.title: One form, two jobs
blocks.text: *Ekmek yanmış!* is a sentence: **the bread has burnt!**, a discovery. *Yanmış ekmek* is a phrase: **burnt bread**. After its noun `-mIş` is a verb; before it, an adjective.

summary: `-mIş` + type I endings: *gelmişim, gelmişsin, gelmiş*; negative *gelmemiş*; question *gelmiş mi?*, *gelmiş misin?*, *gelmişler mi?*
With **I**, it's what you realize only now (*Unutmuşum*); with **you**, surprise (*Çok değişmişsin!*); with **he** or **they**, hearsay and inference.
`-DI` for what you saw, did or know as fact, history included; `-mIş` for what you heard, read, inferred or just found out, legends included.
Reported tenses: tense + `-(y)mIş`: *geliyormuş, gelecekmiş, gelirmiş, gelmeliymiş, gelebilirmiş*; question *geliyor muymuş?*
*-mIşmIş* is colloquial, a report you doubt; *-(I)rmIş* is the habit of folk tales.
Before a noun, `-mIş` is an adjective: *pişmiş tavuk*, *donmuş göl*, *kızarmış ekmek*; *dolmuş* and *geçmiş* are nouns.
